title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 169 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār ends
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 809–810 (Night 169, continuing directly from nights-168), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 169 ends the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The woman who seizes the jeweller's hand is Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl, and she tells him how the Caliph had forgiven her mistress everything, until one evening a singing-girl sang verses of parting at his banquet and Shams al-Nahār fell down dead. The Caliph mourned her and freed her slave-girls. When ʿAlī's funeral comes to Baghdad, the jeweller finds the girl among the mourners; ʿAlī is buried, and the jeweller visits the two graves ever after. Shahrazād closes by promising a tale more wondrous still, that of King Shahramān; the print gives no closing formula for this night. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-ninth night,
sentences.n: al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِيَّ قَالَ وَإِذَا بِامْرَأَةٍ قَبَضَتْ عَلَى يَدِي فَتَأَمَّلْتُهَا وَإِذَا هِيَ الْجَارِيَةُ الَّتِي تَأْتِي مِنْ عِنْدِ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَقَدْ عَلَاهَا الِانْكِسَارُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya qāla wa-idhā bi-imraʾatin qabaḍat ʿalā yadī fa-taʾammaltuhā wa-idhā hiya al-jāriyatu allatī taʾtī min ʿindi Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-qad ʿalāhā al-inkisāru
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said: And behold, a-woman seized on my-hand; and I-looked-closely-at-her, and behold, she (was) the slave-girl who comes from the presence of Shams al-Nahār, and brokenness had mounted-upon-her.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said: All at once a woman caught hold of my hand. I looked at her closely, and it was the slave-girl who used to come from Shams al-Nahār, and she was utterly downcast.
sentences.n: The night picks up the moment where the last one broke off. Two kinds of wa-idhā, “and behold”: in the first, bi- only marks what appears (bi-imraʾatin, “a woman”); the second opens a plain nominal clause, idhā hiya …, “behold, she was …”. taʾammala, Form V, “to look at closely”. taʾtī, imperfect for what she used to do: “who would come”. ʿalāhā al-inkisāru, “brokenness rose over her”, i.e. dejection was written on her. The hamzas of بامرأة, فتأملتها and تأتي are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَعَارَفْنَا بَكَيْنَا جَمِيعًا حَتَّى أَتَيْنَا إِلَي تِلْكَ الدَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taʿārafnā bakaynā jamīʿan ḥattā ataynā ilā tilka al-dāri
sentences.l: And when we-recognised-each-other, we-wept all-together until we-came to that house.
sentences.i: When we knew each other, we both wept, and went on weeping until we reached that house.
sentences.n: taʿārafa, Form VI, “to recognise one another”: the Form VI pattern makes the action mutual. jamīʿan, “all together”, here simply “both of us”. ḥattā, “until”. “That house” is not named; it is presumably the house the jeweller had taken for the lovers' meetings. الي is the print's spelling of ilā, with ي.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا هَلْ عَلِمْتِ بِخَبَرِ الْفَتَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā hal ʿalimti bi-khabari al-fatā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: Did you-(f.)-know of the news of the young-man ʿAlī ibn Bakkār?
sentences.i: I said to her, “Have you heard what happened to young ʿAlī ibn Bakkār?”
sentences.n: ʿalima bi-, “to know of, have word of”: bi- marks the thing one has knowledge of. khabar, “news, what has happened”. al-fatā, “the young man”, in apposition to the name that follows.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَا وَاللَّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lā wa-Allāhi
sentences.l: And she-said: No, by God.
sentences.i: She said, “No, by God.”

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِخَبَرِةِ وَمَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِةِ وَنَحْنُ نَبْكِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhbartuhā bi-khabarihi wa-mā kāna min amrihi wa-naḥnu nabkī
sentences.l: And I-informed-her of his-news and what was of his-affair, and we (were) weeping.
sentences.i: So I told her what had happened to him and all that had befallen him, the two of us weeping as I spoke.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to inform (someone) of”: the verb chooses bi- for what is told. بخبرة and امرة are khabarihi and amrihi, “his news”, “his affair”: the print writes the pronoun -hu/-hi with ة, as often. بخبرة is not bi-khibratin, “with skill”. wa-naḥnu nabkī, a circumstantial clause with wa-: “while we wept”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي قُلْتُ لَهَا وَكَيْفَ حَالُ سَيِّدَتِكِ
sentences.tr: thumma innī qultu lahā wa-kayfa ḥālu sayyidatiki
sentences.l: Then (indeed) I said to-her: And how (is) the state of your-(f.)-mistress?
sentences.i: Then I said to her, “And how is your mistress?”
sentences.n: thumma innī + perfect, “then I …”, the narrator's stock way of moving the story on. The wa- before kayfa is conversational: “and how …?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَمْ يَقْبَلْ أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فِيهَا قَوْلَ أَحَدٍ لِشِدَّةِ مَحَبَّتِهِ لَهَا وَقَدْ حَمَلَ جَمِيعَ أُمُورِهَا عَلَى الْمَحَامِلِ الْحَسَنَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lam yaqbal amīru al-muʾminīna fīhā qawla aḥadin li-shiddati maḥabbatihi lahā wa-qad ḥamala jamīʿa umūrihā ʿalā al-maḥāmili al-ḥasanati
sentences.l: And she-said: The Commander of the Believers did not accept regarding-her the word of anyone, for-the-intensity of his-love for-her; and he-had carried all her-affairs on the good constructions.
sentences.i: She said, “The Commander of the Faithful would not listen to a word from anyone against her, he loved her so dearly; he put the best construction on everything she had done.
sentences.n: qabila fīhā qawla aḥadin, “accepted no one's word about her”: fī here is “concerning”, and in context “against”. li-shidda, “because of the intensity”: li- gives the cause. ḥamala al-amra ʿalā …, “to carry a matter onto (a reading)”, i.e. to interpret it so; al-maḥāmil al-ḥasana, “the good interpretations”, plural of maḥmil, the way a thing is taken. So: he gave her the benefit of every doubt. The hamza of المؤمنين is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ لَهَا يَا شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ أَنْتِ عِنْدِي عَزِيزَةٌ وَأَنَا أَتَحَمَّلُكِ عَلَى رَغْمِ أَعْدَائِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-khalīfatu lahā yā Shamsa al-Nahāri anti ʿindī ʿazīzatun wa-anā ataḥammaluki ʿalā raghmi aʿdāʾiki
sentences.l: And the Caliph said to-her: O Shams al-Nahār, you (are) with-me dear, and I bear-with-you on the spite of your-enemies.
sentences.i: The Caliph said to her, ‘Shams al-Nahār, you are dear to me, and I will stand by you in spite of your enemies.’
sentences.n: Shamsa is accusative after yā because the name is a construct phrase, “Sun of the Day”. ʿindī, “with me”, i.e. in my eyes. taḥammala, Form V, “to bear, put up with, stand by”. ʿalā raghmi, “in spite of”: raghm is the humiliation of being forced against one's will, so “to the chagrin of your enemies”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ لَهَا بِفَرْشِ مَقْصُورَةٍ مُذَهَّبَةٍ وَحُجْرَةٍ مَلِيحَةٍ وَصَارَتْ عِنْدَةُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ فِي عَيْشٍ رَغِيدٍ وَقَبُولٍ عَظِيمٍ
sentences.tr: thumma amara lahā bi-farshi maqṣūratin mudhahhabatin wa-ḥujratin malīḥatin wa-ṣārat ʿindahu min dhālika fī ʿayshin raghīdin wa-qabūlin ʿaẓīmin
sentences.l: Then he-ordered for-her the furnishing of a-gilded chamber and a-fine room; and she-became with-him, from that, in an-easy life and a-great acceptance.
sentences.i: Then he ordered a gilded apartment and a fine room to be furnished for her, and from then on she lived with him in ease and plenty and in high favour.
sentences.n: amara li- … bi-, “to order (something) for (someone)”: the verb takes the thing ordered with bi-, the person it is for with li-. farsh, “furnishing, spreading (of carpets)”. maqṣūra, a private apartment; mudhahhaba, Form II passive participle, “gilded”. عندة is ʿindahu, “with him”, the pronoun again written with ة. min dhālika, “from that (time)”. ʿaysh raghīd, “an easy, plentiful life”; qabūl, “acceptance”, i.e. favour.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُ جَلَسَ يَوْمًا مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ عَلَى جَرْيِ عَادَتِهِ لِلشُّرْبِ وَحَضَرَتِ الْمَحَاظِي بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annahu jalasa yawman mina al-ayyāmi ʿalā jaryi ʿādatihi li-al-shurbi wa-ḥaḍarati al-maḥāẓī bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And it-chanced that he sat one-day of the days, on the running of his-custom, for-the-drinking, and the favourites were-present between his-two-hands.
sentences.i: Now it happened one day that he sat down to drink, as was his custom, and his favourites came before him.
sentences.n: ittafaqa anna …, Form VIII, “it chanced that …”. yawman mina al-ayyām, “one day”. ʿalā jaryi ʿādatihi, “according to the course of his custom”. li-al-shurb, “for drinking”: li- of purpose. al-maḥāẓī, plural of maḥẓiyya, “a favoured one”, the women of the harem whom the master favours. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, i.e. in his presence.

sentences.t: فَأَجْلَسَهُنَّ فِي مَرَاتِبِهِنَّ وَأَجْلَسَهَا بِجَانِبِهِ وَقَدْ عَلِمْتُ صَبْرَهَا وَزَادَ أَمْرُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ajlasahunna fī marātibihinna wa-ajlasahā bi-jānibihi wa-qad ʿalimtu ṣabrahā wa-zāda amruhā
sentences.l: And he-seated-them in their-ranks, and he-seated-her at-his-side; and I had known her-endurance, and her-affair had-increased.
sentences.i: He seated them each in her rank and seated her at his side; and I knew what she was bearing, and how her trouble had grown.
sentences.n: ajlasa, Form IV of jalasa, “to make sit, seat”. marātib, “ranks, places”: each woman sat in her proper order. bi-jānibihi, “at his side”: bi- of place. The clause وقد علمت صبرها is doubtful. As printed it most easily reads wa-qad ʿalimtu ṣabrahā, “and I knew her endurance”, the girl's aside on what her mistress was holding in. The sense would run more smoothly with عدمت, wa-qad ʿadimat ṣabrahā, “she had lost her patience”, one letter-shape away (ل for د); the print is kept and the reading is uncertain. zāda amruhā, “her affair increased”, i.e. her distress grew.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَمَرَ جَارِيَةً مِنَ الْجَوَارِي أَنْ تُغَنِّىَ فَأَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَأَصْلَحَتْهُ وَجَسَّتْهُ وَضَرَبَتْ بِهِ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika amara jāriyatan mina al-jawārī an tughanniya fa-akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-aṣlaḥathu wa-jassathu wa-ḍarabat bihi thumma anshadat taqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And at that, he-ordered a-slave-girl of the slave-girls that she-sing; and she-took the lute, and tuned-it, and felt-it, and struck on-it; then she-recited, saying: Verse.
sentences.i: Then he commanded one of the slave-girls to sing. She took up the lute, tuned it, tried the strings, and began to play; then she sang these lines:
sentences.n: amara … an, “to command (someone) that …”, with the subjunctive. تغنى is tughanniya, Form II ghannā, “to sing”, with the print's ى for ي. aṣlaḥa, Form IV, “to set right”, of a lute “to tune”. jassa, “to feel, touch”: she tries the strings; the shadda of وجسّته is printed. ḍaraba bi-, “to strike with”, of an instrument “to play”: bi- marks the instrument. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”, the stock lead-in to verse, and شعر, “verse”, is the rubric.

sentences.t:
وَدَاعٍ دَعَانِيْ لِلْهَوَى فَاَجَبْتُهُ * وَدَمْعِي يَخُطُّ الْوَجْدَ خَطًّا عَلَى خَدِّيْ
كَأَنَّ دُمُوعَ الْعَيْنِ تُخْبِرُ حَالَنَا * فَتُبْدِى الَّذِي اُخْفِي وَتُخْفِى الَّذِي اُبْدِي
وَقَدْ طَابَ مَوْتِي عِنْدَ فَقْدِ اَحِبَّتِي * فَيَا لَيْتَ شِعْرِي مَا يَطِيبُ لَهُمْ بَعْدِي
sentences.tr:
wa-dāʿin daʿānī li-al-hawā fa-ajabtuhu * wa-damʿī yakhuṭṭu al-wajda khaṭṭan ʿalā khaddī
ka-anna dumūʿa al-ʿayni tukhbiru ḥālanā * fa-tubdī alladhī ukhfī wa-tukhfī alladhī ubdī
wa-qad ṭāba mawtī ʿinda faqdi aḥibbatī * fa-yā layta shiʿrī mā yaṭību lahum baʿdī
sentences.l:
And a-caller called-me to love, and I-answered-him, * while my-tears write the passion, a-writing, upon my-cheek.
As-though the tears of the eye tell our-state: * so they-reveal what I-hide, and they-hide what I-reveal.
And my-death has-become-sweet at the loss of my-beloved-ones; * O would-that (were) my-knowing: what will-be-sweet to-them after-me?
sentences.i:
A caller called me to love, and I answered, while my tears wrote my passion line by line upon my cheek.
It is as if the tears of the eye told our story: they lay bare what I hide, and hide what I lay bare.
Death is sweet to me now that I have lost the ones I love: would that I knew what can be sweet to them when I am gone!
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -dī. The pointing is the print's own and is kept as printed: the bare alif of فَاَجَبْتُهُ and اُخْفِي and اَحِبَّتِي, where the edition marks no hamza, and فَتُبْدِى and وَتُخْفِى with final ى. dāʿin, “a caller”, from daʿā: the indefinite with wa- is the wāw rubba of poetry, “many a caller”, here simply “a caller”. li-al-hawā, “to love”: li- marks the goal of the call. yakhuṭṭu al-wajda khaṭṭan, “writes passion a writing”, the cognate accusative khaṭṭan strengthening the verb: the tears trace the lover's secret on his cheek for all to read. The second line turns on the antithesis abdā / akhfā, “reveal / hide”. ṭāba, “to be pleasant, sweet”. layta shiʿrī, “would that my knowing (were)”, the stock “I wish I knew”. The song fits Shams al-Nahār's own case, parted from her beloved, too closely for her to bear.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ إِنْشَادَ الشِّعْرِ مِنَ الْجَارِيَةِ لَمْ تَسْتَطِعِ الْجُلُوسَ وَسَقَطَتْ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Shamsu al-Nahāri inshāda al-shiʿri mina al-jāriyati lam tastaṭiʿi al-julūsa wa-saqaṭat maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār heard the reciting of the poem from the slave-girl, she-could not (keep) the sitting, and she-fell, fainted upon-her.
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār heard the girl sing the verses, she could not keep her seat, and fell down in a faint.
sentences.n: inshād, verbal noun of Form IV anshada, the singing or declaiming of verse. lam tastaṭiʿi, jussive of Form X istaṭāʿa after lam; the hollow verb loses its long vowel in the closed syllable (tastaṭiʿ), and the kasra is only a linking vowel before al-julūsa. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, the fainting idiom again.

sentences.t: فَرَمَى الْخَلِيفَةُ الْقَدَحَ وَجَذَبَهَا عِنْدَةُ وَصَاحَ وَضَجَّتِ الْجَوَارِي
sentences.tr: fa-ramā al-khalīfatu al-qadaḥa wa-jadhabahā ʿindahu wa-ṣāḥa wa-ḍajjati al-jawārī
sentences.l: And the Caliph threw-down the cup, and drew-her (to) beside-him, and cried-out; and the slave-girls clamoured.
sentences.i: The Caliph flung down his cup, drew her to him and cried out, and the slave-girls raised an uproar.
sentences.n: عندة is the print's spelling of ʿindahu, “beside him”, with tāʾ marbūṭa written for the pronoun ه, a habit of this edition. ḍajja, “to clamour, raise an outcry”, of a crowd; its shadda is printed (ضجّت), and the kasra on the tāʾ is a linking vowel before al-jawārī.

sentences.t: وَقَلَّبَهَا أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَحَرَّكَهَا فَإِذَا هِيَ مَيِّتَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qallabahā amīru al-muʾminīna wa-ḥarrakahā fa-idhā hiya mayyitatun
sentences.l: And the Commander of the Believers turned-her-over and moved-her, and behold, she (was) dead.
sentences.i: The Commander of the Faithful turned her this way and that and shook her, and found that she was dead.
sentences.n: qallaba and ḥarraka, both Form II, “to turn over and over” and “to set moving”; the shadda of each is printed (قلّبها، حرّكها). fa-idhā, “and behold”, the particle of sudden discovery, here followed by a plain nominal clause.

sentences.t: فَحَزِنَ أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لِمَوْتِهَا حُزْنًا شَدِيدًا وَأَمَرَ بِتَكْسِيرِ كُلِّ مَا كَانَ فِي الْمَجْلِسِ مِنَ الْأَوَانِي وَالْعِيدَانِ وَآلَاتِ الْمَلَاهِي وَالطَّرَبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥazina amīru al-muʾminīna li-mawtihā ḥuznan shadīdan wa-amara bi-taksīri kulli mā kāna fī al-majlisi mina al-awānī wa-al-ʿīdāni wa-ālāti al-malāhī wa-al-ṭarabi
sentences.l: And the Commander of the Believers grieved for her-death a grieving severe, and ordered the smashing of all that was in the sitting-room of the vessels and the lutes and the instruments of the diversions and the music.
sentences.i: The Commander of the Faithful grieved bitterly for her death, and ordered everything in the hall to be smashed: the vessels, the lutes, and all the instruments of pleasure and music.
sentences.n: ḥazina … ḥuznan shadīdan, the cognate accusative: the verb's own noun with an adjective, “grieved a severe grief”. li- gives the cause, “for, over (her death)”. taksīr, Form II verbal noun of kasara, “breaking to pieces”: Form II often intensifies. ʿīdān, pl. of ʿūd, the lute. min introduces what “all that was” consisted of.

sentences.t: وَحَمَلَهَا فِي حِجْرِهِ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا وَمَكَثَ عِنْدَهَا بَاقِيَ لَيْلَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥamalahā fī ḥijrihi baʿda mawtihā wa-makatha ʿindahā bāqiya laylatihi
sentences.l: And he-carried-her in his-lap after her-death, and stayed beside-her the rest of his-night.
sentences.i: He held her in his lap after she had died, and stayed by her for the rest of the night.
sentences.n: ḥijr, the lap or bosom, where one holds a child. bāqiya laylatihi, “the remainder of his night”, an accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا طَلَعَ النَّهَارُ جَهَّزَهَا وَأَمَرَ بِغَسْلِهَا وَتَكْفِينِهَا وَدَفْنِهَا وَحَزِنَ عَلَيْهَا حُزْنًا كَثِيرًا وَلَمْ يَسْأَلْ عَنْ حَالِهَا وَلَا عَنِ الْأَمْرِ الَّذِي كَانَتْ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṭalaʿa al-nahāru jahhazahā wa-amara bi-ghaslihā wa-takfīnihā wa-dafnihā wa-ḥazina ʿalayhā ḥuznan kathīran wa-lam yasʾal ʿan ḥālihā wa-lā ʿani al-amri alladhī kānat fīhi
sentences.l: And when the day rose, he-made-her-ready, and ordered her-washing and her-shrouding and her-burying; and he-grieved over-her a grieving much, and did not ask about her-state, nor about the affair which she-was in-it.
sentences.i: When day broke he had her made ready for burial, ordering her to be washed, shrouded and buried. He mourned her deeply, but he never asked about her condition, or about the affair she had been caught up in.”
sentences.n: jahhaza, Form II, “to equip, make ready”, of the dead: to lay out for burial (cf. tajhīz in the night before). ghasl, takfīn, dafn, the three rites in order: washing, shrouding, burial. amara bi-, “to order”: the verb chooses bi- for the thing ordered. al-amr alladhī kānat fīhi, her love for ʿAlī, which the Caliph chooses not to look into. The hamza of يسأل is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ لِلْجَوْهَرِيِّ سَأَلْتُكَ بِاللَّهِ إِلَّا مَا أَعْلَمْتَنِي يَوْمَ وُصُولِ جَنَازَةِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ أَحْضُرَ دَفْنَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālati al-jāriyatu li-al-jawhariyyi saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi illā mā aʿlamtanī yawma wuṣūli janāzati ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin li-ajli an aḥḍura dafnahu
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl said to the jeweller: I-have-asked-you by God, (nothing) but that you-inform-me (of) the day of the arrival of the funeral of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, for-the-sake-of that I-attend his-burial.
sentences.i: Then the girl said to the jeweller, “I beg you by God to let me know the day ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's funeral arrives, so that I may be present at his burial.”
sentences.n: Here the girl's account of the death ends, and the tale steps outside the jeweller's first person for a moment: “the girl said to the jeweller”, where one expects “said to me”. His reply is “he said to her” too; with fa-qumtu, “I rose”, he is “I” again. saʾaltuka bi-Allāhi illā mā + perfect is a fixed adjuration, “I adjure you by God, (I ask) nothing but that you …”: the perfect aʿlamtanī carries the sense of a request, “that you inform me”. janāza, “funeral, bier”. li-ajli an, “in order that”, with the subjunctive aḥḍura. The hamza of سألتك is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَمَّا أَنَا فَفِي أَيِّ مَحَلٍّ شِئْتِ تَجِدِينِي وَأَمَّا أَنْتِ فَفِي أَيِّ مَحَلٍّ أَجِدُكِ وَمَنْ يَسْتَطِيعُ الْوُصُولَ إِلَيْكِ فِى الْمَحَلِّ الَّذِي أَنْتِ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ammā anā fa-fī ayyi maḥallin shiʾti tajidīnī wa-ammā anti fa-fī ayyi maḥallin ajiduki wa-man yastaṭīʿu al-wuṣūla ilayki fī al-maḥalli alladhī anti fīhi
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: As for me, then in whatever place you-wish, you-find-me; and as for you, then in which place do-I-find-you, and who is-able (for) the reaching to-you in the place which you (are) in-it?
sentences.i: He said to her, “As for me, you will find me wherever you please; but as for you, where am I to find you, and who can reach you in the place where you live?”
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … then”, set twice in balance, anā against anti. The marks on امّا and ايّ are printed. ayy is here first conditional (“whatever place you wish”), then interrogative (“in which place?”). تجديني, tajidīnī: in the conditional answer this can be read as the Classical jussive tajidī + -nī; read as a plain indicative it is the colloquial shortening of tajidīnanī, with one nūn dropped. The hamza of شئت is printed; فى is the print's spelling of fī. The girl had lived in the Caliph's palace with Shams al-Nahār, beyond a jeweller's reach.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لَمَّا مَاتَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ أَعْتَقَ جَوَارِيَهَا مِنْ يَوْمِ مَوْتِهَا وَأَنَا مِنْ جُمْلَتِهِنَّ وَنَحْنُ مُقِيمَاتٌ عَلَى تُرْبَتِهَا فِى الْمَحَلِّ الْفُلَانِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu inna amīra al-muʾminīna lammā mātat Shamsu al-Nahāri aʿtaqa jawāriyahā min yawmi mawtihā wa-anā min jumlatihinna wa-naḥnu muqīmātun ʿalā turbatihā fī al-maḥalli al-fulāniyyi
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: Indeed the Commander of the Believers, when Shams al-Nahār died, freed her-slave-girls from the day of her-death, and I (am) of the-number-of-them, and we (are) dwelling-ones at her-tomb in the place such-and-such.
sentences.i: She said to him, “When Shams al-Nahār died, the Commander of the Faithful set her slave-girls free from the day of her death, and I am one of them. We are staying by her tomb, in such-and-such a place.”
sentences.n: aʿtaqa, Form IV, “to set (a slave) free”. min jumlatihinna, “among their whole number”, i.e. one of them. turba, properly “earth, soil”, then a grave or the mausoleum over it. al-maḥall al-fulānī, “such-and-such a place”: the narrator does not name it.

sentences.t: فَقُمْتُ مَعَهَا وَأَتَيْتُ إِلَى قَبْرِهَا وَزُرْتُ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ وَمَضَيْتُ إِلَى حَالِي
sentences.tr: fa-qumtu maʿahā wa-ataytu ilā qabrihā wa-zurtu Shamsa al-Nahāri wa-maḍaytu ilā ḥālī
sentences.l: And I-rose with-her, and came to her-grave, and visited Shams al-Nahār, and went-off to my-state.
sentences.i: So I went with her to her grave, paid my visit to Shams al-Nahār, and went my way.
sentences.n: The jeweller is “I” again. zāra, “to visit”, here the visit paid to the dead at a grave (ziyāra). maḍā ilā ḥālihi, “to go off to one's own affairs”, i.e. to go one's way.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ أَنْتَظِرُ جَنَازَةَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ إِلَى أَنْ جَاءَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal antaẓiru janāzata ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin ilā an jāʾat
sentences.l: And I-did not cease waiting-for the funeral of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, until that it-came.
sentences.i: And I waited, all that while, for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's funeral to come, until at last it came.
sentences.n: lam azal + imperfect, “I did not cease doing”, i.e. “I kept on”. ilā an, “until”. The hamza of جاءت is printed.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَتْ لَهُ أَهْلُ بَغْدَادَ وَخَرَجْتُ مَعَهُمْ فَوَجَدْتُ الْجَارِيَةَ بَيْنَ النِّسَاءِ وَهِيَ أَشَدُّهُنَّ حُزْنًا
sentences.tr: fa-kharajat lahu ahlu Baghdāda wa-kharajtu maʿahum fa-wajadtu al-jāriyata bayna al-nisāʾi wa-hiya ashadduhunna ḥuznan
sentences.l: And the people of Baghdad went-out for-him, and I-went-out with-them; and I-found the slave-girl among the women, and she (was) the-most-intense-of-them (in) grief.
sentences.i: The people of Baghdad came out to meet him, and I went out with them. I found the girl among the women, and she was the most grief-stricken of them all.
sentences.n: kharajat, feminine, with ahl, “people”: a collective noun for people may take a feminine singular verb, treated as a group. lahu, “for him”, i.e. for ʿAlī. The print sets a ḍamma on the second خرجتُ to mark kharajtu, “I went out”, against kharajat just before. ashadduhunna ḥuznan, elative + accusative of specification: “the most intense of them in grief”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَتَّفِقْ فِي بَغْدَادَ جَنَازَةٌ أَعْظَمُ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yattafiq fī Baghdāda janāzatun aʿẓamu minhā
sentences.l: And there-did not chance in Baghdad a funeral greater than-it.
sentences.i: Never had Baghdad seen a greater funeral.
sentences.n: ittafaqa, Form VIII of wafaqa, “to happen, come about”. The verb is masculine though janāza is feminine: allowed when other words stand between verb and subject. aʿẓamu minhā, elative + min, “greater than it”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ نَزَلْ فِي ازْدِحَامٍ عَظِيمٍ حَتَّى انْتَهَيْنَا إِلَى الْمَقْبَرَةِ وَدَفَنَّاهُ إِلَى رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: wa-lam nazal fī izdiḥāmin ʿaẓīmin ḥattā intahaynā ilā al-maqbarati wa-dafannāhu ilā raḥmati Allāhi taʿālā
sentences.l: And we-did not cease in a crowding great until we-came to the graveyard, and we-buried-him (away) to the mercy of God, exalted.
sentences.i: We pressed on through a great crush of people until we came to the graveyard, and there we buried him and gave him over to the mercy of God Most High.
sentences.n: dafannāhu, dafannā + -hu: the nūn of the root and the nūn of “we” merge under a shadda. dafannāhu ilā raḥmati Allāhi, “we buried him (and sent him) to God's mercy”: ilā carries the sense of a verb left unsaid.

sentences.t: وَصِرْتُ لَا أَنْقَطِعُ عَنْ زِيَارَهِ قَبْرِةِ وَقَبْرِ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣirtu lā anqaṭiʿu ʿan ziyārati qabrihi wa-qabri Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And I-became not cutting-myself-off from the visiting of his-grave and the grave of Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: And from then on I never failed to visit his grave and the grave of Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.n: ṣāra + negated imperfect, “I came to be (one who does not …)”, “from then on I never …”. Two spellings of the print cross here: زياره has ه for the feminine ending -a (ziyārati), and قبرة has ة for the pronoun -hu (qabrihi).

sentences.t: فَهَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ حَدِيثِهِمَا رَحِمَهُمَا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-hādhā mā kāna min ḥadīthihimā raḥimahumā Allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: And so this (is) what was of the story of-them-two; may God, exalted, have-mercy-on-them-both.
sentences.i: This, then, is the story of the two of them, may God Most High have mercy on them both.
sentences.n: mā kāna min ḥadīthihimā, “what there was of their story”, the formula that closes a tale. raḥimahumā Allāhu, the perfect used as a wish; -humā, the dual “them both”.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ هَذَا بِأَعْجَبَ مِنْ حَدِيثِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa hādhā bi-aʿjaba min ḥadīthi al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: And this is not more-wondrous than the story of the King Shahramān.
sentences.i: Yet this is no more wondrous than the tale of King Shahramān.
sentences.n: Shahrazād's bridge to the next tale, which the following night takes up. bi- here marks the predicate of laysa and adds emphasis: “this is by no means more wondrous”. aʿjab, elative of ʿajīb, diptote, so it takes fatḥa after bi-; Shahramān, a foreign name in -ān, is diptote too. The print gives no closing formula for the night at this point.
